the five worst times to check your blood
pressure. These are the five moments

your blood pressure to get the most
accurate results possible. Let me start
with the most common mistake that I
literally have conversations about with
patients every single week in primary
care. The worst time at all to check
your blood pressure is in the middle of
the day. This is the one that literally
generates the most unnecessary panic

the middle of all of this chaos, they

that they see sends them into a spiral.
Here is the clinical reality of this
situation. The middle of the day is when
your body is running at its highest
level of physiological demand. Cortisol,
your body's primary stress hormone,
follows a natural daily curve that peaks
in the morning and remains elevated
throughout the middle of the day.
Sympathetic nervous system activity,
that fight or flight system that raises
blood pressure, is at its highest during
active waking hours when the brain is
processing demands, making decisions,
and responding to the environment.
Physical movement throughout the day,
walking between rooms, standing up,
carrying things, all of these produce
constant small fluctuations in blood
pressure that have nothing to do with
hypertension. Pile all of this with the
accumulated stress of a busy morning,
even without a single dramatic stressor,
this produces a sustained cortisol and
adrenaline environment that keeps blood
pressure meaningfully above your true
resting baseline. Research published in
the Journal of Clinical Hypertension
found that blood pressure readings taken
during active daytime hours were
significantly higher and significantly
more variable than readings taken under
standardized resting conditions and that
midday readings produce the highest rate
of false hypertension classification in
home monitoring populations. The
practical fix to this is easy. Do not
check your blood pressure in the middle
of the day at all. Great. Now we're
moving on to the next one. Worst time
number two is to check your blood
pressure within 30 to 60 minutes of
drinking caffeine. Most people check
their blood pressure in the morning,
which is a good thing, but many of my
patients have checked their blood
pressure after their morning cup of
coffee. That is not a good thing. Here's
why. Caffeine is a direct stimulant of
the sympathetic nervous system, that
fight or flight system that raises heart
rate, constricts blood vessels, and
drives blood pressure higher. Within 30
to 60 minutes of consuming caffeine,
systolic blood pressure can rise by
anywhere from 5 to 15 points in
caffeine-sensitive individuals. Some
people are highly sensitive and some
aren't, which means the same cup of
coffee produces a completely different
blood pressure response in different
people. The fix to this is also pretty
easy. Wait at least 60 minutes, but
preferably up to 2 hours or 120 minutes
after taking caffeine before you check
your blood pressure. Before we get into

three to check your blood pressure is
with a full bladder. This surprises
people the most because even if you
don't have to pee right now, you still

affect your blood pressure. A full
bladder activates the sympathetic
nervous system through stretch receptors

Human Hypertension has found that

number four to check your blood pressure
is within an hour of hard exercise. Now,

your blood pressure in the immediate
window after finishing exercising is

here's why. During exercise, the heart

minute and blood pressure rises
substantially, sometimes to even 180 or
up to 200 systolic in healthy adults
during intense effort. Now, blood
pressure will drop in the first 3 to 5
minutes after complete rest of
exercising, but it won't quite get down
to baseline until 60 minutes after the
exercising is done. What makes this even
more nuanced is that blood pressure
readings in this window, the 30 to 60
minutes after exercising, can be
paradoxically high in some people
because of residual sympathetic
activation that hasn't fully resolved or
paradoxically low in others because
post-exercise vasodilation temporarily
drops blood pressure below resting
baseline. Either way, the reading does
not represent your true resting
cardiovascular state. The simple fix is
to wait at least 60 minutes until
exercising is done before checking your
blood pressure. Now, the fifth worst
time on our list is actually not a
specific time at all. It's the single
most important one on this entire list,
and that is only taking a single
reading. One single blood pressure
reading has enormous natural
variability. Blood pressure fluctuates
constantly throughout the day in
response to breathing patterns, posture
changes, ambient temperature, the last
thing you thought about, and dozens of
other physiological variables. A single
reading captures one moment in that
constant fluctuation, and that single
moment may land anywhere on the spectrum
meaningfully above, or perhaps below,
your actual stable baseline. The person
who gets a reading of 158 and panics,
and then takes a second reading of 134 2
minutes later and is confused, is
experiencing the normal moment-to-moment
variability of blood pressure. Neither
reading may be wrong, both are real, and
neither one will tell you the complete
story. The protocol that I recommend to
my patients is this. Sit quietly for a
full 5 minutes. Keep your feet flat on
the floor, empty your bladder, keep your
arm at heart level, and no talking. Take
two readings 1 minute apart, and then
take the lower of those two readings.
When you do this day after day after
day, you then take the average of all of
those numbers, and that is your true
baseline. Now, we talked about the five
